subject: MS
question: State all the three classifications of Wesley's understanding of human nature and briefly explain each of them.
idealAnswer: Wesley's doctrine of man draws on both the Western and Eastern Christian traditions, both of which held that humanity was created in God's image, and his understanding of human nature can be classified under three main themes. The first is humanity as God's gracious creation. It was the free grace of God that formed man from the dust of the ground and breathed into him a living soul, and the state of man before the Fall was complete perfection. Man is a complex being composed of both body and spirit, and Wesley discussed man created in the image of God under three images: the natural image, a spirit endued with understanding, will and liberty; the political image, in which man is God's vice-regent with dominion over the lower creation; and the moral image, in which man was holy, merciful and perfect as God is, which for Wesley was the principal image. The second theme is humanity as fallen. Adam fell first as a result of unbelief, a lack of trust in God, and Eve believed a lie, giving more credit to the word of the Devil than to the Word of God; so for Wesley the nature of human sin is not pride but unbelief, out of which pride, self-will and every other evil disposition flow. The Fall brought not only physical death but pain, sickness and unholy tempers, and while the natural and political images were polluted or lost in part, the moral image was totally lost. The third theme is humanity as freshly restored. The beginning of the work of salvation in any human being is God's prevenient grace, which goes before any human action and enables a response; by justification we are pardoned, saved from the guilt of sin and restored to the favour of God, and by sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin and restored to the image of God, so that the individual is renewed and grows into the whole image of God.
keyPoints: Wesley's doctrine of man rests on both Western and Eastern Christian traditions, which held that humanity was created in God's image
Three themes: humanity as God's gracious creation, humanity as fallen, humanity as freshly restored
Gracious creation: free grace formed man of dust and breathed in a living soul; before the Fall man's state was complete perfection; man is body and spirit
The image of God under three images – natural, political and moral, the moral being the principal image
Humanity as fallen: Adam fell through unbelief, not pride; Eve believed a lie
The natural and political images were polluted or lost in part, the moral image totally lost
Humanity as freshly restored: prevenient grace begins the work, justification pardons and restores to God's favour
Sanctification saves from the power and root of sin and restores the image of God

markingRubric.description: Explains restoration through prevenient grace, justification (saved from the guilt of sin and restored to God's favour) and sanctification (saved from the power and root of sin and restored to the image of God).

subject: MS
topic: John Wesley and the Use of Money
question: State the three formulated rules by Wesley to guide his followers on handling worldly goods and explain each of them.
idealAnswer: Wesley formulated three simple rules to guide his followers on handling worldly goods: “Gain all you can, Save all you can and Give all you can.” He cited two reasons for the rules: most Christians did not know how to deal rightly with money and no one gave them instruction, and the improper use of so valuable a good as money, entrusted to human beings by God, could have far-reaching consequences for both Christians and their neighbours. The first rule, gain all you can, was a challenge to earn as much money as possible, but only through honest means. The second rule, save all you can, exhorted the Methodist to save money in private treasuries or in Bank of England savings accounts and to refrain from all unnecessary spending; money in itself is neither good nor evil, for in the hands of God's children it becomes nourishment for the hungry, drink for the thirsty and clothing for the naked, and all that money can achieve, good or evil, depends on how people use it. The first two rules are only justified through the third, give all you can. Wesley drew a boundary between what a person needed to keep and what he needed to give away: anyone whose income exceeded the necessities of life and personal obligations should give the excess to meet the needs of others. Those who observe the first two rules and not the third are twofold more the children of hell than ever they were before, for it is only the observance of the third rule, which sets forth the social obligations of possessions, that can convert an increasing income into a blessing.
keyPoints: Wesley formulated three simple rules for handling worldly goods
Gain all you can, Save all you can, Give all you can
Two reasons: Christians did not know how to deal rightly with money and were not instructed; the improper use of money has far-reaching consequences
Gain all you can – earn as much as possible, but through honest means
Save all you can – save in private treasuries or Bank of England accounts and refrain from unnecessary spending; money is neither good nor evil
Give all you can – give away all above the necessities of life and personal obligations
Those who keep the first two rules and not the third are twofold more the children of hell than before
Only the third rule converts an increasing income into a blessing

subject: MS
question: What practical intervention did Wesley put in place as a remedy for poverty alleviation?
idealAnswer: From his own savings Wesley provided the basic capital of a loan fund from which the poor could take interest-free loans for up to three months. The loan amount was first limited to twenty shillings but was later raised to five pounds, and within one year more than 250 persons had been provided with loans, thus saving them from money lenders who demanded exorbitant interest. Alongside this, because many poor people could not secure medicine or the aid of a physician, Wesley himself dispensed medicine and treated simple illnesses, freely aiding some hundreds of people, most of whom did not even belong to any of the Methodist societies.
keyPoints: Wesley provided the basic capital of a loan fund from his own savings
The poor could take interest-free loans for up to three months
The loan was first limited to twenty shillings, later raised to five pounds
Within one year more than 250 persons had received loans
This saved them from money lenders who demanded exorbitant interest
He also dispensed medicine and treated simple illnesses free of charge

subject: MS
question: Which people resisted Wesley's work in the prisons?
idealAnswer: Wesley's work in the prisons was resisted by the prison authorities and by pastors. He was refused permission to converse with some who had been condemned to death, even though the prisoners themselves had requested it, and in Bristol his daily worship service was limited to one sermon a week.
keyPoints: Wesley's work in the prisons was resisted by prison authorities
It was also resisted by pastors
He was refused permission to converse with some condemned prisoners who had asked for him
In Bristol his daily worship service was limited to a sermon per week

subject: MS
chapter: JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH IN JESUS CHRIST
question: According to Wesley, “by justification we are saved from the guilt of sin and restored to the favour of God”. What does he say of sanctification?
idealAnswer: Wesley wrote: “By sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin and restored to the image of God.” He added that all experience, as well as Scripture, shows this salvation to be both instantaneous and gradual: it begins the moment we are justified and increases gradually from that moment, as a grain of mustard seed which is at first the least of all seeds but afterwards puts forth large branches and becomes a great tree, until in another instant the heart is cleansed from all sin and filled with pure love to God and man; and even that love increases more and more till we attain the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.
keyPoints: By sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin
And restored to the image of God
The salvation is both instantaneous and gradual
It begins the moment we are justified
It grows like a grain of mustard seed into a great tree
Until the heart is cleansed from all sin and filled with pure love to God and man

markingRubric.label: Restored to the image of God
markingRubric.description: States that by sanctification we are restored to the image of God, and may add that it is both instantaneous and gradual, beginning the moment we are justified.

subject: MS
question: Apart from Wesley's preaching and advocacy for prisoners, what other significant thing was done for the prisoners?
idealAnswer: Wesley secured a good number of the Methodists to care for prisoners. They visited the prisoners to read the Bible and pray with them, submitted petitions to the authorities on their behalf, comforted and encouraged them, and accompanied condemned prisoners to the scaffold, sparing them the hooting of crowds eager for a spectacle. Money was also collected in the Methodists' worship service to buy the prisoners clothing, food and mattresses.

They visited to read the Bible and pray with them
They submitted petitions to the authorities on the prisoners' behalf
They comforted and encouraged them
They accompanied condemned prisoners to the scaffold, avoiding the hooting of crowds
Money was collected in Methodist worship services to buy clothing, food and mattresses

subject: MS
chapter: THE BASIS OF WESLEY'S THEOLOGICAL THINKING
question: What is found in Wesley's journal for May 14, 1765?
idealAnswer: In his Journal for May 14, 1765 Wesley writes: “In 1730 I began to be Homo Unius Libri, to study comparatively no book but the Bible.” John Wesley called himself Homo Unius Libri – a man of one Book – for he possessed a passionate love for Scripture and presented a theology of Scripture that affirmed its divine inspiration, never doubting its trustworthiness and allowing no other rule, whether of faith or practice, than the Holy Scriptures.
keyPoints: The entry is in Wesley's Journal for May 14, 1765
“In 1730 I began to be Homo Unius Libri, to study comparatively no book but the Bible”
Homo Unius Libri means a man of one Book
It expresses Wesley's passionate love for Scripture and his affirmation of its divine inspiration

markingRubric.label: Its meaning
markingRubric.description: Explains that Homo Unius Libri means a man of one Book, expressing Wesley's supreme regard for Scripture.

explanation: Tests the well-known Journal entry in which Wesley calls himself a man of one Book.

subject: MS
question: The Wesleyan revival showed much social responsibility for certain categories of people. State three of such categories. (i) … (ii) … (iii) …
acceptedAnswers: The poor – Wesley gave away his income, dispensed medicine and set up an interest-free loan fund for them
Prisoners – Wesley preached and prayed in the London and Bristol prisons and organised Methodists to care for them
Slaves – Wesley published his Thoughts upon Slavery and supported the campaign for abolition
Those harmed by the liquor trade
explanation: The syllabus introduces this sentence and then treats the groups in turn: the poor (including his teaching on the use of money), slaves, prisoners, and those harmed by the liquor trade.
